To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ubiquitin ligase MID1 is actively transported along the microfilaments and that this transport depends on both the MAP kinase signaling cascade and on the activity of PP2A, which is in turn regulated by the regulatory subunit α 4.

(1) the MID1 ubiquilin is actively and bidirectionally transported along the cytoskeletal microtubules; (2) this movement is directly regulated by the protein phosphatase PP2A; and (3) this mechanism is disrupted in patients with Opiz BBB/G Syndrome carrying mutations in the MID1 gene.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying the Opitz BBB/G Syndrome.
the molecular mechanisms that regulate the stability of microtubules in the cell.
the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie the development of ventral midline structures and their malformations in Opitz BBB/G Syndrome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the MID1/PP2A/alpha4 complex is a MAPK substrate and that the phosphorylation state of MID1 is critical for its active transport along microtubules.
the active transport of MID1 is regulated by PP2A, and that this transport depends on the interaction of MID1 with its regulatory α4 subunit.
the MID1 protein complex is actively transported along microtubules by a kinesin- and dynein-mediated mechanism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MID1 is a novel MAP kinase substrate that undergoes a dynamic phosphorylation-dependent transport along the cytoskeletal microtubule network.
the active transport of MID1 along microtubules is regulated by protein phosphatase PP2A and that the active transport is inhibited in OS patients with B-box-1 mutations.

PP2A/ α4/MID1 is a novel microtubule associated protein that is actively and dynamically transported along the micro tubules, and that its active movement depends on the phosphorylation status of MID1.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the microtubular transport of MID1 is a regulated process that requires the interaction of MID1 with the regulatory subunits of PP2A and is controlled by the MAP kinase pathway and PP2A.
the active transport of MID1 is directly linked to the phosphorylation state of MID1 by PP2A.
the active transport of MID1 along the microtubes is a dynamic process regulated by PP2A, and that this transport is required for the proper localization of MID1 at the centrosome.
